chunks: Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya from al-Hasan ibn Musa al-Khashshab from Ghiyath ibn Kalub from Isḥaq ibn 'Ammar from Ja'far from his father (peace be upon them both)

A mukatab (a slave who has contracted to pay a sum for his freedom) came to Ali (peace be upon him) and said: 'My master contracted with me and stipulated installments (nujum) to be paid each year. I brought him the entire money in one lump sum, and asked him to accept it all at once and validate my freedom, but he refused. Ali (peace be upon him) called him and said: 'He is truthful.' Then Ali (peace be upon him) asked him: 'Why do you not accept the money and validate his freedom?' He said: 'I only accept the installments that I stipulated, so that I may be exposed to inheriting him [if he dies before the full amount is paid].' Ali (peace be upon him) said: 'You are more entitled to your stipulation.'

Because the first report only included permitting the taking of his money from the installments in one lump sum, and did not include that it is obligatory for him to accept his money before the time, and the latter report included that he has the right to refuse accepting it and to demand it according to what he stipulated for him, and there is no contradiction between them in any case.

key_terms.عِتْق: Manumission or freeing of a slave
key_terms.مُكَاتَب: A slave who has entered a contract with his master to pay a specific sum for his manumission
key_terms.نُجُوما: Installments or periodic payments (plural of najm)

ai.seo_question: Can a master refuse lump-sum payment from a mukatab to preserve inheritance rights?
ai.summary: Imam Ja'far al-Sadiq (AS) affirms the master's right to refuse early lump-sum payment to preserve his inheritance share, a ruling validated by Ali (AS) as 'he is more entitled to his condition.' This highlights the principle of contractual autonomy in *kitabah*, where the master is not obligated to accept early settlement if it diminishes his potential inheritance, resolving apparent contradictions in juristic reports. The narration underscores the flexibility of Islamic commercial law in balancing the slave's desire for freedom with the master's financial interests.
